earlier_scan.source_named: Only Hooley & McElhanon 1970 (Morobe survey/classification) cited on Glottolog; archive.org has only a Swadesh list (rosettaproject_mhf_swadesh-1); no phonological description found.

sources.citation: Rice, Amy. 2024. Orthography and Phonology Data: Finongan Language. SIL-PNG. 13 pp. (current version of the Finongan OPD).
sources.note: Would supersede the 2010 OPD for the variety Mamaa speakers now use (Finongan, fino1238), not for Mamaa itself.
sources.venue: SIL-PNG. 13 pp. (current version of the Finongan OPD)

sources.citation: Pennington, Ryan. 2014. Ma Manda Phonology. SIL e-Books 64. Dallas: SIL International. [= A's work 0, re-listed per checker protocol because the open-but-silent work does carry Erap-family-level prosody sentences that A's note denied; they do not name Mamaa]
sources.note: Family-level only: no Erap language has been analysed as tonal; Nek, Finongan and Uri are reported (second-hand) to have word-initial quantity/quality-sensitive stress like Ma Manda; Numanggang's claimed contrastive stress is reinterpreted as heavy-syllable attraction. Nothing on Mamaa.

sources.citation: Rice, Chris & Amy Rice. 2010. Finongan Organised Phonology Data. Ukarumpa: SIL-PNG. 12 pp. [Finongan fag / fino1238, which lists Mama among its major villages]
sources.note: For FINONGAN, not Mamaa: p. 6 Suprasegmentals 'Contrasting tones or tone patterns are not in evidence. Stress is unpredictable but non-contrastive. Closed syllables and syllables with lengthened vowels are often but not always stressed.' Relevant only as the language Mamaa speakers are shifting to.

sources.citation: Greenhill, Simon J. (ed.). transnewguinea.org: Language Mamaa (55 lexical items from McElhanon & Voorhoeve 1970).
sources.note: Wordlist only (no stress marks in the transcriptions).

sources.citation: OLAC: resources in and about the Mamaa language [mhf] (catalog as of 2025-02-13).
sources.note: Lists only Rosetta Project Swadesh list, transnewguinea.org, Glottolog and Ethnologue entries; no description, no SIL archive item.

sources.citation: Pawley, Andrew & Harald Hammarstrom. 2017. The Trans New Guinea family. In Bill Palmer (ed.), The Languages and Linguistics of the New Guinea Area: A Comprehensive Guide, 21-195. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton. (OAPEN open-access chapter; archive.org item oapen-20.500.12657-23719).
sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: Nothing on Mamaa; it is a source census. Neighbour entries: Finongan [fag] 'minimal: Rice and Rice 2002', Gusan 'comparative studies', Numanggang 'specific feature: Hynum 2010', Mungkip/Nakama 'wordlist: Retsema et al. 2009'.
sources.venue: The Languages and Linguistics of the New Guinea Area: A Comprehensive Guide

sources.citation: Hammarström, Harald & Sebastian Nordhoff. 2012. Online appendix to 'The languages of Melanesia: quantifying the level of coverage'. In N. Evans & M. Klamer (eds), Melanesian languages on the edge of Asia (LD&C Special Publication 5), 13-34. Honolulu: University of Hawai'i Press.
sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: coverage inventory only: entry lists Claassen & McElhanon 1970 and Smith 1988 only; no stress/tone statement (database of descriptive coverage, not a description)
sources.venue: Melanesian languages on the edge of Asia (LD&C Special Publication 5)

sources.citation: ISO 639-3 Registration Authority. 2008. Change Request 2008-023 (R. Hiley & C. Rice, SIL-PNG): proposed merge of [mhf] Mamaa into [fag] Finongan (rejected 2009-01-16).
sources.note: Nothing. Sociolinguistic rationale only (1997: 75% lexical similarity with Finongan; Mamaa villagers 'reported that they used to speak a different language'); cites Troolin & VanderWal 1997 unpublished Finongan preallocation survey.

sources.citation: Carrington, Lois. 1996. A linguistic bibliography of the New Guinea area. Pacific Linguistics D-90. Canberra: Australian National University.
sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: bibliography only: survey/classification works only

sources.citation: Smith, Geoffrey P. 1988. Morobe counting systems. Papers in New Guinea Linguistics 26, 1-132. Pacific Linguistics A-76. Canberra: Australian National University.
sources.note: Nothing. The volume is about numeral systems; its transcription note defines only a schwa symbol ('an unaccented neutral vowel') and c for glottal stop; the six 'stress' hits in the text are all the English verb ('stressed by Ray', 'Dutton stresses'). No prosodic marking on the Mamaa numerals.

sources.citation: McElhanon, Kenneth A. 1984. A linguistic field guide to the Morobe Province, Papua New Guinea. Pacific Linguistics D-57. Canberra: ANU. iv+80 pp.
sources.note: No phonology content: classification, village lists with census populations, travel/mission notes and a general bibliography; the author explicitly declines to give phonetic values for vernacular spellings (p. 31).

sources.citation: McElhanon, Kenneth A. 1975. North-Eastern Trans-New Guinea Phylum languages. In S. A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea area languages and language study, vol. 1: Papuan languages and the New Guinea linguistic scene, 527-567. Pacific Linguistics C-38. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Nothing. The phonology section tabulates segmental phonemes for Kate, Ono, Selepet, Kube, Nabak, Urii, Wantoat, Kewieng, Rawa, Kovai; notes voiceless/voiced(prenasalised) stop contrast, labio-velars, six-vowel pattern, vowel length 'not a common feature', simple syllable structure with p t k m n ng codas. No sentence on stress, accent, tone or pitch anywhere in the chapter (a full-text search for stress/accent the text: 0 hits).
sources.venue: New Guinea area languages and language study

sources.citation: McElhanon, Kenneth A. 1973. Towards a typology of the Finisterre-Huon languages, New Guinea. Pacific Linguistics B-22. Canberra: ANU. viii+80 pp.
sources.harvard_location: Divinity School Library (offsite storage), call number - Ask at Circulation (Pamph. folio) BS 354 .Z91
sources.note: Mamaa appears only in the Erap family member list (p. vi). Phonology ch. 1 (pp. 5-8) covers ten representative languages (Uri for Erap) and has no stress/accent statement at all.

sources.citation: Claassen, Oren R. & Kenneth A. McElhanon. 1970. Languages of the Finisterre Range - New Guinea. Papers in New Guinea Linguistics 11, Pacific Linguistics A-23: 45-78. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Mamaa entry sec. 2.7.1 (pp. 56-57) is population/lexicostatistics only (pop. 200, 46% with Finungwan, being assimilated, mostly bilingual). Phonology sec. 6.1 (pp. 63-67) uses Uri as the Erap representative; its only stress sentence (p. 67): 'Stress is phonemic in Rawa but probably sub-phonemic in Yupna and Wantoat. In none of these languages does it carry a heavy functional load.. In Suroi stress is contrastive, but only on a limited number of words.' Nothing on Mamaa or Erap stress.
sources.venue: Papers in New Guinea Linguistics 11, Pacific Linguistics A-23: 45-78

sources.citation: Hooley, Bruce A. & Kenneth A. McElhanon. 1970. Languages of the Morobe District - New Guinea. In S. A. Wurm & D. C. Laycock (eds), Pacific linguistic studies in honour of Arthur Capell, Pacific Linguistics C-13: 1065-1094. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Nothing. Mamaa p. 1073: 'a small language of one village on the banks of the lower Irumu River. The Mamaa speakers are gradually being assimilated by the Finungwan people and most of them are bilingual'; checklist no. 33 (pop. 200). Classification/lexicostatistics only.
sources.venue: Pacific linguistic studies in honour of Arthur Capell, Pacific Linguistics C-13: 1065-1094

sources.citation: McElhanon, Kenneth A. & C. L. Voorhoeve. 1970. The Trans-New Guinea Phylum: explorations in deep-level genetic relationships. Pacific Linguistics B-16. Canberra: Australian National University. 107 pp.
sources.note: Nothing: comparative wordlists in phonetic spelling without stress marks; whole-text search for stress/tonal/accent/pitch = 0 (the 6 'tone' hits are all 'stone'). Wordlist only for Mamaa.
